subject: alienFlora
pitch:
Category: Plant.
Subject: bioluminescent alien plant.
Style: Avatar.

spec.name: Sylvaglow Lumibloom
spec.description: A towering Pandora-style bioluminescent alien plant: a spiral helicoradian-like stalk crowned by a glowing bell flower, drooping tendril fronds, big fan leaves, and glowing ground pods and roots.
spec.layout: Centred on x=0. A buttress root base with glowing veins sits on the floor. From it rises a slightly curved, ribbed trunk leaning gently toward +Z. At mid-height two large fan leaves spread left and right. At the top a big bell-shaped flower with a ring of petals opens upward, with a glowing core and floating spores. Long drooping tendrils with glowing tips hang from a crown ring below the bell. Small glowing pods and mushrooms sit at the base. Avatar style: deep indigo and teal bodies with cyan, magenta and violet glowing dots, veins and rims, all as small parts in their own flat colours; glow() is used on all luminous bits.

parts.builds: Ground footprint: soil mound disc, 6 buttress roots flaring outward as tapered sweeps in bark colours with cyan glowing veins along them, small glowing pods (magenta, green, violet spheres) and little mushroom lamps scattered around, moss patches in moss colour, and glowing ground dots.
parts.attaches: Trunk starts at baseTop; rides root joint.

parts.builds: Ribbed spiral trunk from baseTop to trunkTop as a sweep with bark/barkDark/barkLight bands, 8-sided faceted section tapering from radius 0.4 to 0.22, a spiral of small glowing cyan dots and a twisting vein ribbon winding up it, knobbly bumps, and a collar ring at crownRing.
parts.attaches: Starts at baseTop, ends at trunkTop/crownRing; leaves attach at trunkMid, flower at flowerBase.

parts.builds: Two huge mirrored fan leaves (extruded outlines with scalloped edges, leafTeal with leafDeep underside) spreading left and right from leafRingL at mid trunk, arching upward then drooping, each with a central rib and branching cyan veins as thin parts, glowing rim dots in magenta and violet, plus two smaller secondary leaves per side.
parts.attaches: Roots at trunkMid; rides leafL, leafR.

parts.builds: Top bell flower at flowerBase: lathe-turned bell cup in petalPink, 10 broad extruded petals ringed around and flaring outward with petalLight tips and cyan vein lines, an inner ring of smaller violet petals, a glowing coreWhite/magenta core orb, stamens as thin rods with glowing tips, and about 20 small floating glowing spore spheres above the flower.
parts.attaches: Sits on trunkTop at flowerBase; rides flowerHead.

parts.builds: About 14 long drooping tendrils ringed around crownRing, each a thin tapering sweep in bark/violet bands curving outward then down to near the ground at varying lengths, with glowing tip bulbs in cyan, magenta and green, and small glowing beads along their length; one ring of tiny hanging bell buds under the collar.
parts.attaches: Root at crownRing; rides tendril1 and trunk3.

calls.reasoning:
I'm planning a buildFlowerCrown function using the SDK, favoring safe geometry APIs like lathe, extrude, and sweep for the crown structure plus a glow effect, while figuring out how the Ctx type is supplied by the module without needing an explicit import.

Now I'm working out the lathe outline for the bell-shaped flower cup, mapping out coordinate points that flare outward from the axis then curve back inward to form a hollow shell with thickness, making sure the outer and inner walls don't intersect and the loop closes cleanly along the axis.

For the petals, I'm figuring out how to extrude each one by defining a local coordinate frame per petal angle: a radial direction outward from the stem, a tangential width direction, and a leaning axis that tilts the petal outward and upward from vertical to get the flared, drooping look.

I'm positioning the petals flaring outward from the bell's middle at a steep angle, checking the geometry fits within the bounding box with room to spare. Now I'm planning a separate, slightly larger tip piece in a lighter color to overlay the petal ends for visual depth.

Computing vein placement using tangent/axis/normal vectors for each petal, with a central vein and side branches offset slightly from the surface, and tallying up part counts per petal across the flower.

Now I'm budgeting total parts: bell, rim ring, outer petals (10×5), inner petals (8×2), core/halo/magenta ring, stamens (12×2), spores (20), bell veins and rim beads, aiming for roughly 170 pieces. I'll apply glow effects to veins, stamen tips, spores, and the core using the palette colors.

I'm setting up the extrusion geometry so petal thickness runs along orthogonal tangent and axis vectors anchored to the flower head bone, using rod and sphere primitives for veins and nodes with flat shading. Now I'm placing the smaller violet inner petals at a tighter radius around the center.

Still designing petal placement...

I'm scaling each petal's outline by length and width factors, giving inner petals lighter glowing tips, and adding curved stamen rods rising from the core with magenta and green glowing tips, topped by a glowing white and magenta core sphere at the flower's center.

Now I'm switching the solid magenta shell to a thin torus ring around the core instead, checking that stamens and inner petals fit properly within the bell's interior without poking through the walls too much.

I'm placing scattered spore particles in a disc above the flower, randomizing their position, size, and cycling through cyan, magenta, green, violet, and white colors, while verifying everything stays within the bounding box.

For the rim, I'm adding a thin glowing torus ring plus small beaded spheres around it, then sweeping thin veins along the bell's outer curved profile using polylines rather than many individual rod segments to keep the geometry lightweight.

I'm also adding a collar of sepals at the base with a small torus ring and a lathe-based cup bottom, then starting to write the petal helper function that builds each petal from its angle and shape parameters.

Still writing petal function...

Working out vein placement on the inner concave face, using the negated normal to position them slightly embedded with a half-thickness around 0.012, and setting up points spanning along the leaf length for the vein rods.

Adding branch veins now, running from roughly a quarter down the length outward to points near the edges around 0.6 of the length, before writing out the final geometry.

I'm planning the buildTendrils function, laying out around 14 tendrils spaced around the crown ring that curve outward and downward using bezier paths within the defined bounding box.

Each tendril gets its own small joint chain (3 joints) parented to J.tendril1, keeping the total joint count safely under the 160 limit. I'll sweep a tube mesh along each chain with a radius function for tapering, add a bulb part at the tip bone, and scatter beads along the sweep surface using points sampled from the chain.

Now I'm plotting the actual path geometry: each tendril starts at a ring point around the torso center, extends outward along a direction vector, and arcs upward with randomized length and reach, while clamping the outward radius so endpoints stay within the bounding box. I'm also checking whether glow effects apply cleanly to stick-based parts, confirming they return standard Part objects compatible with flat color strings.

I'm considering adding small spherical knobs at the base of each tendril to mark where they emerge from the trunk's collar ring, plus a slight spiral sway offset that varies with height for a more organic look.

Now I'm designing a ring of tiny hanging bell buds beneath the collar, lathing each bell's profile curve so it opens downward with a glowing tip bead, being careful the outline points don't self-intersect.

I'm settling on a couple of custom violet shades for the tendril and bell, then designing the tip bulbs with glowing cyan/magenta/green spheres topped with a small bark-cup sheath and a white highlight for extra depth.

For the tendril's sweep, I'm tapering the radius from thick at the base to thin near the tip with a faceted six-sided profile, then scattering small beads alternating left and right along the curve with a cycling cyan/magenta/green/violet glow, possibly adding tiny spike details for texture.

I need to budget the part count carefully: with sweep, bulb pieces, beads, and spikes multiplied across 14 tendrils plus buds, I'm way over the 170-part limit, so I'm trimming beads down to 4 and dropping extra spikes, cutting color bands from 3 to 2 per tendril to bring the total closer to around 170-180 parts.

Now I'm settling on 10 parts per tendril times 14 plus 8 buds at 2 parts each, landing at roughly 156 total, which fits the budget, and checking that bead spheres stay low-poly enough to keep triangle counts reasonable. I'm working out how to structure the chain joints and naming convention for each tendril segment so they parent correctly under the tentacle group.

Still defining color bands and tip geometry...

Still working out positions...

Working out the radial reach and endpoint heights for each tendril, alternating longer and shorter ones for variation, then defining a point helper that offsets position around the crown ring center with slight outward swirl and rise, keeping everything within the bounding box.

Refining the outward-arch radius profile for p2, then checking joint counts stay under budget with a 3-segment catmull resample. Now I'm planning the bell bud placements around the trunk, spacing ten buds at a fixed radius and height with stem rods extending outward.

Still adjusting bell placement and sizing...

Finalizing the structure...

I'm defining the buildTrunk function using the shared Ctx type, then planning the trunk's path through its base and segment points.

I'll sweep the trunk mesh along that catmull curve using the trunk joints as the bone chain, giving it a tapering radius from thick at the base to narrow near the top. For texture, I'm adding ribbed bark detail using an octagonal cross-section with darker sector strips spaced every 45 degrees to simulate bark ridges, layered with lighter and darker bands for color variation.

For the magical accent, I'm planning a spiral of 36 glowing cyan dots wrapped around the trunk's surface, placing each by sampling the trunk's curve parameter and rotation angle so they wind upward in a continuous helix, sized relative to the trunk's radius at that point.

Then I'm working out a vein-like ribbon that follows the same spiral path, lifted slightly off the trunk surface using the normal direction, built as a smooth curve through sampled points with a thin glowing cyan sweep—though I need to sort out which bone the resulting geometry should attach to since raw sampled points don't carry bone info by default.

I'll add a second thinner violet spiral offset 180 degrees for contrast, then scatter knobbly low-poly bark bumps across the trunk surface (avoiding the very top and bottom), mixing in a few small glowing violet nubs. For the collar ring near the crown, I'm considering a surface loop sweep to form the ring geometry.

Placing a torus for the collar ring, orienting its axis to match the trunk's tangent direction at that point near the top, sized slightly larger than the trunk radius there...

I'll bump the ring radius to 0.31 so beads sit on the lathe surface, and pass an explicit bone (trunk3) to the stick options since that overrides the ring item's default bone. I'm also considering adding a lower bark-swell collar around y=0.6 as a root-sleeve transition, plus maybe a mid-trunk ring, but keeping it modest for now.

For the leaf attachment zone around y=1.5–1.6, I'll add a swollen node ring with a slightly larger radius, computing its position by finding the closest path parameter to that point so the tangent lines up correctly. I need to make sure this node doesn't clip the leaf geometry since leaves start from inside the trunk anyway. I'm also checking that everything fits within the bounding box constraints for x, y, and z, confirming the trunk radius keeps the z-range valid.

Now I'm working through the cap geometry at both ends of the trunk path: a round cap would extend the trunk below the box's minimum y or above its maximum y, so I'm switching to flat caps on both ends instead, relying on the flower base and buried roots to visually cover the flat transitions, and starting the path exactly at the box's y minimum.

Laying out the Catmull-Rom control points along the trunk from base to flower head, I'm assigning joint positions and bone segments (trunk1, trunk2, trunk3), then defining a tapering radius array and a color banding scheme that blends bark tones along the length.

I realize the full 16-sector-per-band scheme would blow past my mesh budget across all pieces, so I need to cut down to just a handful of dark groove sectors instead of covering every face and vertex.

Reducing further: 3 bands with 8 dark sectors each gives 27 meshes for this piece, keeping the overall part budget around 140 once dots, bumps, ribbon, collar, and nodes are factored in. I'm now working out the spiral dot placement, spacing roughly 44 dots with angle incrementing by 1080/t plus alternating offsets.

Placing colors cyan-dominant with occasional magenta and violet glow accents, positioning dots and ribbon along slightly offset spiral angles so they don't collide, with the ribbon lifted outward along the normal at roughly 2.5 turns.

For bumps, I'm scattering hit points across the trunk's surface within a height range, filtering out overlaps near the ribbon/dots, and sizing each bump as a flattened icosahedron with slight random scale variation.

Every fourth bump gets a tiny glowing violet nub stuck just above it for visual interest, and I'm adding a swelling lathe-shaped node partway up the trunk to break up its silhouette.

I'll space the ring items evenly around the circle but skip the ones near 90/270 degrees where they'd collide with the leaves, using 12 slots and excluding two indices. For the collar near the top, I'm finding the path point closest to around y=2.45 and sketching its lathe outline shape.

Now I'm adding a glowing cyan ring using a thin torus aligned along the z-axis, positioned slightly above the collar center along the tangent direction, plus a scatter of magenta beads arranged radially outward at that same height, checking that the collar still fits within the bounding box limit.

Then I'm shaping the bottom sleeve flare as a lathe profile in dark bark coloring, widening the base silhouette while keeping it inside the x and z bounds, and adding a thin glowing cyan band around it using a reusable torus-ring helper function parameterized by position, radius, tube thickness, color, lift, and glow strength.

I'm assigning bones to the trunk segments by height threshold, setting up a seeded random generator for the scatter placement, and sweeping the trunk path with octagonal cross-section, bark coloring, and darker colored bands at specific points along it.

Now I'm adding dark sector markings at 45-degree intervals around the trunk for a bark-plate look, and considering thin glowing cyan slits on some faces as a decorative crack detail.

I need to write buildBaseRoots using the Ctx type provided by the module scope, destructuring the needed fields from it and following the existing template pattern rather than importing a separate type.

I'm planning a soil mound as a lathed disc hub blending into the trunk base, plus six buttress roots built as sweeps along catmull paths that flare outward from the trunk and taper down to meet the ground, all attached to the root joint with lighter bark coloring near their tips.

Positioning the six roots at evenly spaced angles with jitter and varied lengths within the box limits, then adding thin glowing cyan vein sweeps that trace along the top surface of each root, with some smaller branching veins coming off them for extra detail.

Scattering glowing magenta dots along the sweep paths with small sphere sticks, then tallying up the part budget: soil, hub, roots, veins, and dots come to roughly 44 parts. I'm sketching the pods as glowing icosahedrons with darker calyx bases, and planning the mushroom lamps with stem cylinders and lathe caps.

Adding rim glow rings, moss patches, ground dots, and small violet rootlets between the roots brings the running total to around 146, comfortably under the 170 budget. Now I'm working out placement angles so roots don't overlap, spacing them at 30+60i degree intervals around the mound.

I'm defining a radial height function for the mound surface so pods, mushrooms, and ground discs sink naturally into the terrain rather than floating above it, matching the lathe outline profile from the base edge inward.

For the sweep's orientation, I should pass an explicit up vector so the tube frame doesn't flip unpredictably along the path, keeping the normal roughly aligned with world up for these horizontal-ish root segments.

Now I'm shaping the buttress root curve itself: it starts near the trunk base around radius 0.12-0.2, curves outward and downward through control points toward the tip, tapering from an elliptical cross-section (rx~0.17, ry~0.13) down to a thin end, with the base partially buried into the hub lathe shape for a natural merge.

I'm also planning the surface vein details -- thin sweep lines along the root following the surface normal with a slight lift, sliced to avoid the very ends, using a small circular cross-section with reduced polygon sides for a subtle faceted look, plus setting up a glow element.

I'm deciding on vein coloring, mainly cyan with a few violet accents, and planning small glow spheres embedded at a few points along the root's length offset at an angle to suggest branching light. I'm also starting on the pod shape using a low-detail icosahedron for a flattened, faceted bulb form.

Each pod cluster gets a darker cone-shaped calyx cup beneath it plus a tiny bright highlight sphere on top, bringing the part count per pod to three, and I'm moving on to designing the mushroom stem next.

Each mushroom has stem, cap, gill disc, and two spots, so I'm trimming to 7 mushrooms at 5 parts each to stay within budget. Tallying everything up — soil, hub, roots, pods, mushrooms, moss, ground dots — I land around 155 parts, comfortably under the 170 cap, so I'm good to proceed with moss patches as flattened, scaled icosahedron spheres scattered across the mound.

Adding 20 ground dots and setting up a seeded RNG function for scatter placement. Now I'm defining the hub as a lathe shape with a bark-colored profile tapering upward, using 8 segments for the trunk base.

Still writing geometry...

Placing pod coordinates...

Settling on mushroom placements at 20, 70, 130, 170, 235, 310, 350 degrees with varying radii, keeping them far enough from pod positions to avoid overlap. I'm checking distances between pods and mushrooms at each angle pair to confirm spacing works, then deciding to slightly enlarge the pod radii beyond the initial small 0.06-0.12m range.

Bumping mushroom proportions up too, and deciding on a glowing-cap lamp design with alternating violet/magenta/cyan caps, bright core spots, and dropping the gill disc in favor of simpler stem-cap-spot geometry for four parts per mushroom across seven mushrooms.

Writing mushroom geometry code...

For the mound I'm lathing a soil-colored outline with 16 segments, keeping it simple and dark since moss patches will add the visual interest on top. Now I'm moving to root generation, building a helper function that computes points along a curved path using sine/cosine offsets for radius and height.

Still writing root path points...

Adding sector colors and vein line placement, deciding on sides count for the roots geometry and vein angle positions along the surface.

For moss, I'll pre-scale a flattened sphere geometry rather than relying on a scale option in the stick helper, giving it that squashed clump look. For ground elements I'll use positioned parts attached to the root bone with rotation for tilt, and for pods I'm using icosahedron geometry placed just above ground with flat shading, thinking through a cylinder-based calyx shape underneath.

Now I'm working out pod highlight placement, offsetting a small glowing sphere toward the upper-front of each pod using a normalized direction vector, and starting to design the mushroom stem geometry with a slight tilt rotation.

Shaping the mushroom cap as a lathe profile and positioning glowing spots across its dome surface...

Placing the glow core sphere at the spot location, then adding ground elements: moss tuft cones scattered near the base and flat scaled moss patches with randomized rotation for natural coverage.

I'll skip the bridging veins and rootlets but add a hub glow rim, confirming the mound sits flush at y=0. Now writing the final code, using a helper tuple type for positions and a seeded RNG for deterministic placement, with the glow function accepting colors from the part definitions.

I'm planning out a buildFanLeaves function for this part, thinking through how each leaf on left and right sides should be shaped as an extruded outline with scalloped edges, arching upward from the base positions.

Since flat extrusion can't bend, I'm considering membranes between rib and rim paths to get a naturally curved leaf -- a petiole stalk arching outward then drooping, with a fan blade of radiating lobe membranes at the end. For the underside color, I'll layer a thinner offset membrane beneath the main blade to get the two-tone teal/deep coloring, and now I'm working out the midrib curve's coordinates along the leaf's length.

I'm thinking of each blade ray as radiating fan-like from the petiole point across a spread of angles, with each wedge between adjacent rays forming a lobe whose outer edge gets scalloped, varying ray lengths to shape the overall fan outline.

Still computing ray geometry...

Adding the deep underside layer offset slightly below center for a subtle proud effect, then planning the midrib sweep from petiole to tip with tapering radius for a vein-like structure.

Working out the centre ray relation to the midrib: each vein's horizontal position maps to an equivalent u along the midrib, so its droop follows yM at that scaled u. I'm defining the midrib as a catmull-rom spline through six points, bound to joint leafL for bone inheritance.

For veins, each of the 9 rays per leaf becomes a thin glowing cyan sweep tapering from radius 0.012 to 0.005, and I'm adding secondary branch spikes at t=0.45 and 0.7 along each ray using thin rods toward the adjacent ray direction.

I'm realizing the branching math needs a helper function to compute any point along a ray at a given angle and parameter so I can place these side branches accurately, but doing this for every ray at every offset would blow past my part budget—so I'm cutting branches down to just two points per ray on each side, and tallying up total parts (petiole, rib, membranes) to stay near 190.

Adding 8 smaller scallop-rim dots brings each primary leaf to 17 dots, totaling 60 per side or 120 overall. Then I'm sketching secondary smaller fan leaves with fewer rays and dots, which pushes the total past budget, so I need to scale back the counts.

Simplifying to single cross-vein rods per wedge at one t-value gets primary down to 47 elements per side (94 total), with secondary at 76, totaling 170 — leaving room for extras like a bark sleeve collar where petioles meet the trunk and small glow beads per side.

Now I'm placing the secondary leaves: two per side, attaching to the trunk at lower and upper heights, angled outward at roughly 45° front and back with smaller scale than the primary leaves.

I'm generalizing the leaf builder into a reusable function taking origin, yaw, length, width, rise, and branch count, computing forward and lateral directions in the local frame based on the yaw angle.

Working out the midrib curve height profile, tuning the quadratic coefficients so the arch peaks around u≈0.42 and fits within the bounding box without exceeding the floor or ceiling constraints.

Checking secondary leaf placement with 45° yaw to confirm it stays within the bounding box both forward and backward, then working out the fan origin and ray lengths for that leaf.

Working out the ueq formula so the side ray's distance along the midrib direction maps correctly, with L0 as 0.7 of total length, plus a droop factor for cupped edges. Now building each ray's spline points using Catmull-Rom interpolation across four sample positions.

Setting up the membrane surfaces using these edge curves, passing scallop and bone joint parameters with a fixed thickness and a small underside y-offset for the blade's belly.

Now I'm planning the petiole-to-rib sweep as two connected segments: a woody petiole stub with tapering radius leading into a glowing midrib that lifts slightly above the blade surface as it runs toward the tip.

For attachment, the petiole base sits buried inside the trunk radius, so I'm adding a small sheath sphere at the junction for a natural swelling. Then I'm placing tip dots along each ray (alternating magenta/violet glow spheres) plus smaller mid-wedge dots partway along the primary rays for extra detail.

Tallying the part counts: primary leaf runs about 52 elements (membranes, rays, petiole, rib, cross veins, tip and mid dots, sheath), secondary leaves add roughly 19 each, keeping the whole composition comfortably under the part budget. I'm using low-poly flat spheres for the dots with a glow multiplier applied to the ray elements.

Drafting the ray vein sweeps now — positioning them centered on each wedge edge, lifted slightly above the surface, with tapered radii and a reduced side count for a low-poly look, then starting the cross-vein rod connecting from a point along each ray.

For colors, I'm leaning toward adding a secondary leaf teal tone plus the existing palette for ribs, undersides, petiole, and sheath, keeping it consistent with named palette entries rather than inventing new hexes.

I decide against an extra rim or glow trim along the leaf tips since the scalloped edge already handles it, and move on to origin mounts: setting ring positions per side using the mirrored leaf joints and choosing the correct bone reference based on sign.

Writing imports and setup code...

Writing the leaf-building function...

Defining ray geometry...

Checking the side ray math at t=1 confirms the peak height works out fine, but I notice the overall shape forms an inverted bowl since the sides stay high while the center droops — not the natural fan curve I want. I should increase the droop factor for side rays so the silhouette curves more naturally instead of cupping upward.

I'm generating the angle list for n rays spread across the arc, then writing the membrane-building loop that connects each pair of adjacent rays with colored, scalloped surfaces and their underside counterparts.

Now I'm working out the central midrib sweep, extending the ray path to the tip with a tapered radius and a glowing cyan vein running along it.

Then I'm constructing the petiole as a curved sweep from the base through a few intermediate points up to the fan root, tapering its thickness and giving it a bark-like color, plus adding a small sheath sphere at the base scaled flatter to anchor the primary stem.

For the cross veins, I'm connecting adjacent rays at a third/two-thirds point with thin rods, and for the radiating veins I'm sweeping each ray as a curve while skipping the central one when the ray count is odd.

I'm placing tip dots at the end of each ray with size and color varying between primary and secondary rays, plus glow, and then adding mid dots between rays that get pulled inward to create a scalloped edge effect along the lobe surface.

The chord midpoint sits at a slightly lower radial distance than the mid-ray due to the angular step, which works fine. Now I'm setting up the secondary leaves—five of them with reduced length and scale, no cross veins or mid dots—positioning lower and upper pairs with yaw angles around ±50° to angle them toward the back, and adjusting their origin heights accordingly.

Checking the droop calculations, both the lower and upper secondary leaf tips stay comfortably above the minimum height threshold. There's a minor concern about the lower secondary leaf's yaw sweep potentially overlapping with the primary leaf near the root, but it looks like only slight acceptable interpenetration rather than a real collision. I'm also considering whether the primary leaf needs a forward yaw bias rather than staying at zero.

I'm settling on a slight yaw adjustment of 6 degrees for the primary, confirming the secondary petiole starts correctly inside the trunk radius, and finalizing the dot colors as magenta and violet glow tones. The membrane geometry works out to a reasonable triangle count, and I'm adding helper values for underside thickness and a small downward offset vector before skipping the optional root hub bead and writing the final structure.
